title: Slow performance with encryption on an Intel Xeon E5-2407
body:
### System information
Distribution Name	| Proxmox
Distribution Version	| 8.0 (Debian 12)
CPU | Intel Xeon E5-2407
Kernel Version	| 6.2.16-10-pve
Architecture	| x86_64
OpenZFS Version	| 2.1.12-pve1

### Describe the problem you're observing
On an encrypted pool/dataset with 3 VDEVs of 2 mirrors each on SATA SSDs there is a performance issue with AES-256-GCM encryption.

Test with sequential `fio --filename=test --sync=1 --rw=read --bs=4k --numjobs=1 --iodepth=4 --group_reporting --name=test --filesize=1G --runtime=300 && rm test` : 
- With ZFS encryption : 66 MB/s
- Without ZFS encryption : 400MB/S

The CPU has both AES-NI and AVX extensions (aesni_intel module loaded).

### Describe how to reproduce the problem
With an Intel Xeon from the Sandybridge era : 
- Create a zpool with default AES-256-GCM encryption
- Benchmark with fio (or any other software)

### Include any warning/errors/backtraces from the system logs
No useful logs.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> I would guess either "it's just bad" or #15223 is related or both.

Just to confirm. I am not using RAIDZ, only mirrored vdevs (like a RAID10). Also, my CPU has only AVX, no AVX2.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Stupid question: Why is your fio benchmark so slow in the first place even without encryption? You says 400 MB/s for a fio filesize of 1GB. Such a small filesize should fit into cache and be much faster. 

When I do this same fio benchmark on my desktop PC with a 2x2 raid10 with four WD 4 TB drives I get speeds beyond 1500 MB/s. Simply because this all happens in the cache. What is your RAM size resp. zfs cache size?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:

With a simple vdev mirror (2x1 SSD) I have around 400-560 MB/s. Cannot test on the 3x2 SSD RAID10 without destroying data (I think so ? My zpool is encrypted).

> When I do this same fio benchmark on my desktop PC with a 2x2 raid10 with four WD 4 TB drives I get speeds beyond 1500 MB/s. Simply because this all happens in the cache. What is your RAM size resp. zfs cache size?

32GB or RAM. Arc size currently around 7GB, but it can go up to 16GB.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: If you want to simulate performance on small files, you should reduce dataset's recordsize too.  Otherwise small I/O, especially random and especially writes, over the file with large recordsize may be a disaster and not even close to your workload.  Though I am not saying that your encryption speed is not a problem, more that even your base line may be too low.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
You should use the zfs recordsize as the fio blocksize. If recordsize is 128k you should use --bs=128k. 

I suggest you set recordsize=1M and --bs=1M. This will give you the maximum performance of your system. No matter what your use case is. This will show you what is possible with your hardware.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
This output tells me two things: 
1) Your 2x1 SSD, Mirror is as fast as I would expect. 895 MB/s is good
2) the latency when using encryption is huge:
`lat (usec): min=326, max=367669, avg=22152.62, stdev=21146.29`
That is 20 times slower than  without encryption (avg=1160.15)

I would say that this confirms that your CPU is really slow with encryption which adds a lot of wait time to the read operation. 

Now the question is if this is zfs specific or if other encryption solutions have the same issue. You might want to do another fio benchmark with a luks partition or with an gocryptfs container.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
For reference, on Ubuntu 5.15.0-75-generic (missing the aforementioned FPU rework patch, so far), with 2.1.12:
```
$ grep . /sys/module/icp/parameters/*
/sys/module/icp/parameters/icp_aes_impl:cycle [fastest] generic x86_64 aesni
/sys/module/icp/parameters/icp_gcm_avx_chunk_size:32736
/sys/module/icp/parameters/icp_gcm_impl:cycle [fastest] avx generic pclmulqdq
```

So that does, indeed, seem like it's probably at least a problem, if not the problem.

Something I noticed when digging into someone else's very similar issue, was that, when their livecd ran very fast and their installed environment ran very poorly on the exact same hardware, monitoring where it was spending its time showed a lot of time in the FPU enter/exit functions in ZFS on the slow env, and virtually none at all on the fast one.

So what I'm wondering is, does the bug in Linux make the "stop everything" calls we make to safely implement the FPU calls ourselves more expensive? I think we'd probably need to like, rip apart a kernel with and without that bug, and the associated compiled module, to know, or build versions of each with full symbols since I think the trace showing where the time is spent is just getting elided otherwise.
